title: Reading a medicine pot or oral measure
blurb: Work out the scale on a medicine pot, read the bottom of the meniscus at eye level and record the volume dispensed in Pearson format.
question: A 30 mL medicine pot is marked every 2.5 mL, with numbers at 10, 20 and 30. The bottom of the meniscus is level with the third mark above 10. What volume has been dispensed?

teach.h: The second picture on the paper
teach.body: Item 2 of every Part A practice paper shows a medicine pot and asks what volume has been dispensed. A medicine pot (oral measure) is a small graduated cup, usually 30 mL, marked every 5 mL or every 2.5 mL. Plain English: the method is the same as a syringe (work out what each mark is worth, then count) but the liquid surface curves, so you must read at the right point.

teach.h: Read the bottom of the meniscus
teach.body: Liquid in a pot curves up at the edges; this curve is the meniscus. Read the volume at the bottom of the curve, with the pot on a flat surface and your eye level with the liquid. Looking down from above (parallax) makes the level look wrong.

head: Pot
Numbers
Marks every
teach.caption: Check the picture each time: the gap between numbers and the number of spaces set the value of each mark.

items: Midwife Hannah Clarke pours an oral liquid for a woman. The 30 mL pot has numbers at 10, 20 and 30, with marks every 2.5 mL.
Each space: 10 mL between numbers ÷ 4 spaces = 2.5 mL.
At eye level, the bottom of the meniscus is on the third mark above 10.
Sense check: three of the four spaces between 10 and 20 is three quarters of the way, so 17.5 mL fits.

teach.text: Reading the top of the meniscus, or looking down from above, gives a reading that is too high. And do not assume every mark is 5 mL: many pots are marked every 2.5 mL. Volumes smaller than the pot's marks, or not a multiple of them, need an oral syringe.

items.label: trailing zero: not the accepted form

items: Pot on a flat surface, eye level with the liquid.
Read the bottom of the meniscus.
Value per mark = gap between numbers ÷ spaces.
Volume = number below + spaces x value.
Small or awkward volumes need an oral syringe.

summary: You can now work out the scale on any medicine pot, read the volume at the bottom of the meniscus at eye level, find how much more to add or remove, and record the result in Pearson format.

A.q: A 30 mL medicine pot has numbers at 10, 20 and 30, with marks every 2.5 mL. The bottom of the meniscus is level with the third mark above 10. What volume has been dispensed? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: Counted each mark as 1 mL; they are 2.5 mL.
whyNot.1: Counted each mark as 5 mL; they are 2.5 mL.
whyNot.3: Counted two spaces; the meniscus is on the third mark.

A.q: In a medicine pot, the edges of the liquid curve up to the 12.5 mL mark, while the bottom of the meniscus is level with the 10 mL mark. What volume is in the pot? Please use the correct unit.
A.why: The volume is read at the bottom of the meniscus: 10 mL.

whyNot.0: This is the top of the curve; read the bottom of the meniscus.
whyNot.2: Averaged the two levels; read the bottom of the meniscus.
whyNot.3: This is the height of the curve, not the volume.

A.q: A 60 mL oral measure has numbers every 10 mL and marks every 5 mL. The bottom of the meniscus is level with the unnumbered mark between 20 and 30. What volume is in the measure? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.0: Counted the mark as 2.5 mL; on this measure it is 5 mL.
whyNot.1: Counted the mark as 1 mL; it is 5 mL.
whyNot.2: Read the next numbered mark instead of the mark below it.

B.q: A child is prescribed 12.5 mL of an oral antibiotic. The pot, marked every 2.5 mL, currently holds 15 mL. How much must be removed? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
B.why: 15 - 12.5 = 2.5 mL to remove. Discard the excess: dispensed liquid is not poured back into the stock bottle.

whyNot.0: Removing 5 mL would leave 10 mL, not 12.5 mL.
whyNot.1: Added the two volumes; the excess is the difference.
whyNot.2: This is the dose, not the amount to remove.

B.q: A woman is prescribed 15 mL of lactulose. The pot has numbers every 5 mL and marks every 2.5 mL. How many small marks above the 10 mL number should the bottom of the meniscus reach?
B.why: 15 - 10 = 5 mL. 5 ÷ 2.5 = 2 marks above 10 (which is also the 15 mL number).

whyNot.3: Counted 2.5 mL marks from zero: 15 ÷ 2.5 is 6, but the count starts at 10.

B.q: A 30 mL medicine pot has 12 equal spaces between 0 and 30 mL. What volume does each space represent? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.2: Divided 12 by 30; divide the volume by the spaces.

C.q: A child is prescribed 300 mg of an oral suspension. The bottle label reads 200 mg in 5 mL. What volume should be poured into the pot? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
C.why: 300 ÷ 200 x 5 = 7.5 mL. A pot marked every 2.5 mL can measure this.

whyNot.2: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.3: Right number, wrong unit: the answer is a volume in mL.

C.q: A woman was given 17.5 mL in a pot marked every 2.5 mL with numbers every 5 mL. Afterwards the bottom of the meniscus is level with the second mark above 5. How much has she taken? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.0: Read the second mark above 5 as 15 mL; it is 10 mL.
whyNot.1: Counted each mark as 1 mL, giving 7 mL left.
whyNot.3: This is what is left, not what she has taken.

C.q: Looking down at a pot held in the hand, the liquid seems to reach 15 mL. With the pot on a flat surface at eye level, the bottom of the meniscus is level with 12.5 mL. What volume should be recorded? Please use the correct unit.
C.why: Read at eye level, pot on a flat surface, at the bottom of the meniscus: 12.5 mL.

whyNot.0: This reading was distorted by looking down from above.
whyNot.1: Averaged two readings; record the eye-level reading.
whyNot.3: This is the error between the readings, not the volume.

reteach.title: Crouch, then count
reteach.question: Why does a medicine pot need to be on the table rather than in your hand?

blocks.body: A tilted pot moves the liquid, and looking down from above makes the line look higher. Put the pot on a flat surface, crouch so your eye is level with the liquid, and read the lowest point of the curve. Then count marks up from the numbered line below.

blocks.text: Pots marked every 2.5 mL look very like pots marked every 5 mL. Work out the mark value every time.

explain.body: Gap between numbers ÷ number of spaces. 10 mL ÷ 4 spaces = 2.5 mL.

test.q: A pot is numbered at 10, 20 and 30 mL, with 4 equal spaces between each pair of numbers. What does each space represent? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.

whyNot.1: Gave the number of spaces as the volume.
whyNot.3: Divided 4 by 10; divide the gap by the spaces.

explain.body: The liquid creeps up the sides; ignore that and read the lowest point.

test.q: The bottom of the meniscus is level with 20 mL, and the edges of the liquid climb to 22.5 mL. What volume is in the pot? Please use the correct unit.
test.why: Read the bottom of the meniscus: 20 mL.

whyNot.0: This is where the edges reach; read the bottom of the curve.
whyNot.2: This is the height of the curve, not the volume.

explain.body: Find the numbered mark below the meniscus and add the marks above it.

test.q: A pot is numbered at 10, 20 and 30 mL, with a mark every 5 mL. The bottom of the meniscus is level with the unnumbered mark between 0 and 10. What volume is in the pot? Please use the correct unit.

whyNot.0: Counted the mark as 2.5 mL; on this pot it is 5 mL.
whyNot.2: Counted the mark as 1 mL; it is 5 mL.

explain.body: Significant digits only, leading zero below 1, unit mL with no s.

test.q: A pot holds twenty-two and a half millilitres and the question asks you to use the correct unit. Which answer is in the correct format?
test.why: 22.5 mL: significant digits only and the standard abbreviation.

whyNot.1: The trailing zero is not the accepted form.
whyNot.3: Fractions are not accepted; use a decimal point.
